title: JAGG: Jacobian-Aggregated Group Gradient for Efficient GRPO Training of Diffusion Models

paper.title: JAGG: Jacobian-Aggregated Group Gradient for Efficient GRPO Training of Diffusion Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is a powerful reinforcement learning algorithm for aligning generative models with human preferences. While successful in large language models ( Shao et al. 2024 ) , its extension to diffusion and flow matching models introduces a severe computational bottleneck: gradients must be back-propagated through the high-capacity DiT backbone at every timestep of the sampling trajectory, making high-resolution text-to-image (T2I) training prohibitively expensive. Training-free DiT inference acceleration methods (e.g., Δ \Delta -DiT, ScalingCache) exploit the fact that DiT hidden states and velocity predictions vary smoothly and nearly linearly along the trajectory. We ask whether the same linearity can reduce the backward-pass cost of DiT RL training, and answer affirmatively with JAGG ( J acobian- A ggregated G roup G radient), which reduces full transformer backward passes from W W to 2 2 per group of W W consecutive steps. JAGG approximates intermediate-step Jacobians via t t -weighted interpolation of the endpoint Jacobians, then aggregates per-step upstream signals into two composite gradients applied through a single joint backward pass. We prove this interpolation is exact when the velocity is linear in ( z , t ) (z,t) , and a cosine-similarity routing rule ( jagg_frac ) deploys JAGG only where the assumption holds. Experiments on T2I benchmarks show JAGG delivers ∼ \sim 2 × \times backward speedup with negligible quality degradation.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has recently emerged as a compelling reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm for aligning generative models with human feedback and reward signals. Initially proposed in the context of large language models (LLMs) ( Shao et al. 2024 ) , GRPO eliminates the need for a separate value network by normalizing advantages within a group of candidate responses sampled from the same policy. This design significantly reduces the memory and computational overhead compared to Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), making online RL training practical for large-scale autoregressive models. The success of GRPO in mathematical reasoning ( Shao et al. 2024 ) , long-context tasks ( Ping et al. 2026 ) , and multimodal alignment ( Wang et al. 2026b ) has spurred interest in extending the paradigm beyond language. More recently, GRPO has been adapted to diffusion-based visual generation, where it has shown promising results in improving image quality, text alignment, and aesthetic preference. Two pioneering works—DanceGRPO ( Xue et al. 2025 ) and Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al. 2025a ) —demonstrated that applying GRPO to diffusion transformers (DiTs) and flow matching models can substantially enhance generation quality. Both methods treat the denoising process as a multi-step decision-making problem, computing a policy gradient loss at each timestep of the sampling trajectory. However, this per-step formulation introduces a severe computational bottleneck: standard training requires one full forward + backward pass through the denoising network for every timestep in each training window. For high-resolution text-to-image (T2I) generation, where sampling trajectories typically span dozens of steps, this leads to prohibitively expensive training. The key distinguishing feature of DiT RL, compared to language model RL, is that the “actions” are entire high-dimensional denoising steps, and the policy must be optimized over long multi-step trajectories that unfold through the DiT backbone. This structure imposes an unavoidable requirement: gradients must be back-propagated through the denoising network at every timestep of the trajectory in order to update model parameters. Unlike language models, where each token step is lightweight, each backward pass through a modern DiT incurs the full cost of a transformer forward pass, making the per-step backward requirement the dominant training expense . Interestingly, this same trajectory structure has been extensively studied in the context of training-free DiT inference acceleration. A line of work has observed that the hidden states, attention outputs, and velocity predictions of DiTs vary smoothly and nearly linearly along the denoising trajectory : consecutive denoising steps produce similar intermediate representations that can be reused, cached, or extrapolated with minimal quality loss. Methods such as Δ \Delta -DiT ( Chen et al. 2024b ) , Pyramid Attention Broadcast ( Zhao et al. 2025b ) , TaylorSeers ( Liu et al. 2025b ) , and ScalingCache ( Gu et al. 2026 ) all exploit this trajectory smoothness to skip or approximate network evaluations at intermediate timesteps, achieving substantial inference speedups with negligible quality degradation. This raises a natural question: can the same trajectory linearity that benefits training-free inference acceleration also be exploited to reduce the backward-pass cost in DiT RL training? If the Jacobians of the denoising velocity field with respect to model parameters vary linearly along the trajectory—mirroring the observed smoothness of the forward activations—then the expensive per-step backward passes could be replaced by cheap interpolations, reducing the total number of full network backward passes from W W to a small constant. In this work, we address the efficiency challenge of diffusion GRPO training. We propose JAGG ( J acobian- A ggregated G roup G radient), a mathematically principled acceleration method that reduces the number of network backward passes from W W to 2 2 for a group of W W consecutive denoising steps. Our key insight is that the Jacobian of the denoising velocity field v θ ​ ( z , t ) v_{\theta}(z,t) with respect to model parameters θ \theta is approximately linear in the inputs ( z , t ) (z,t) during the high-noise regime, which permits accurate interpolation of intermediate-step Jacobians from only the endpoint Jacobians. We provide a formal proof that this interpolation is exact when the velocity is strictly linear, and demonstrate empirically that the approximation holds with negligible error under practical training conditions. We validate JAGG on T2I benchmarks, demonstrating consistent acceleration with negligible degradation in generation quality. Our contributions are: • We identify and formalize the computational bottleneck in diffusion GRPO training, arising from per-timestep backward passes across the sampling trajectory. • We propose JAGG, a Jacobian-aggregation framework that reduces backward passes from W W to 2 2 per group, grounded in a rigorous theoretical analysis of the linearity of velocity Jacobians. • We prove that under linear velocity conditions, the t t -weighted Jacobian interpolation is exact with zero approximation error. • We demonstrate the generality of our method through extensive experiments on text-to-image generation tasks across multiple diffusion backbones.

sections.heading: Related Work
sections.text: Diffusion, Flow Matching, and RL Fine-tuning. Diffusion models ( Ho, Jain, and Abbeel 2020 ; Song, Meng, and Ermon 2022 ) and rectified-flow matching ( Liu, Gong, and Liu 2022 ) underpin modern visual generation, with surveys of their interplay with RL in ( Zhu et al. 2024 ; Du et al. 2024 ) . Early RL-based fine-tuning frames denoising as a multi-step decision process (DDPO ( Black et al. 2024 ) ), and follow-ups explore preference optimization (DPOK ( Fan et al. 2023 ) , DiffPO ( Chen et al. 2025 ) ), KL-regularized PPO (DiffPPO ( Xiao et al. 2024 ) ), text-encoder RL (TexForce ( Chen et al. 2024a ) ), and diversity-oriented RL ( Miao et al. 2024 ) . GRPO for Visual Generation. DanceGRPO ( Xue et al. 2025 ) and Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al. 2025a ) first adapted GRPO to diffusion/flow models, with follow-ups on unified reasoning-driven optimization (UniGRPO ( Liu et al. 2026 ) ), stability via branching (BranchGRPO ( Li et al. 2025 ) ) or clip regulation (GRPO-Guard ( Wang et al. 2025 ) ), ODE/SDE mixing (MixGRPO ( Li et al. 2026 ) ), credit assignment (PCPO ( Lee and Ye 2026 ) ), and extensions to masked ( Luo et al. 2026 ) , autoregressive ( Yuan et al. 2025 ) , and discrete ( Wang et al. 2026a ; Ma et al. 2025 ) generators, video RL ( Zheng et al. 2026b ) , simplified online RL for denoisers (V-GRPO ( Tang et al. 2026 ) ), forward-process alignment (DiffusionNFT ( Zheng et al. 2026a ) ), likelihood-estimation design ( Choi et al. 2026 ) , and black-box distillation (PRISM ( Wang et al. 2026b ) ). Beyond images, GRPO has also been applied to diffusion language models ( Zhong et al. 2026 ; Rojas et al. 2026 ; Zhao et al. 2025a ) . Existing accelerations of the GRPO backward pass—stochastic backward in DanceGRPO ( Xue et al. 2025 ) , restricted SDE windows in Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al. 2025a ) and MixGRPO ( Li et al. 2026 ) , and merged trajectories in BranchGRPO ( Li et al. 2025 ) —are heuristic and discard much per-step gradient information; we instead faithfully approximate the full backward-pass signal at a substantially lower cost. GRPO in Language Models. GRPO originated in DeepSeekMath ( Shao et al. 2024 ) and was later extended to long-context reasoning ( Ping et al. 2026 ) and connected to classification-style RLVR ( Zhai et al. 2026 ) ; see ( Zhang et al. 2025 ) for a broader survey. Unlike inference-time acceleration (distillation, consistency models), our work is orthogonal and targets the backward-pass bottleneck specific to diffusion GRPO.

sections.heading: Memory-Efficient Implementation Variants
sections.text: The joint-backward variant described above (Algorithm 1 ) builds computation graphs for both endpoints simultaneously and issues a single torch.autograd.backward call, which is optimal for FSDP communication. However, for very large models with billions of parameters, two live computation graphs may exceed GPU memory budget. We therefore provide a second sequential-graph variant (Algorithm 2 ) that processes the two endpoint graphs one at a time: 1. Run no-grad forward for the middle W − 2 W{-}2 steps and accumulate partial s base s_{\text{base}} / s corr s_{\text{corr}} contributions. 2. Run with-grad forward for j = 0 j{=}0 ; compute s 0 s_{0} via proxy and add to s base s_{\text{base}} ; call v ^ 0 . backward ​ ( s base ) \hat{v}_{0}.\texttt{backward}(s_{\text{base}}) immediately. The graph for step 0 is freed before step W − 1 W{-}1 is ever built. 3. Run with-grad forward for j = W − 1 j{=}W{-}1 ; compute s W − 1 s_{W-1} via proxy and add to s corr s_{\text{corr}} ; call v ^ W − 1 . backward ​ ( s corr ) \hat{v}_{W-1}.\texttt{backward}(s_{\text{corr}}) . The sequential variant keeps at most one computation graph in memory at any time, at the cost of two separate FSDP all-gathers (one per backward). In practice we use the joint variant for T2I models, reserving the sequential variant for cases where peak memory is critical. Both variants produce identical gradients and achieve the same ∼ \sim 2 × \times backward speedup. The full pseudocode for both variants is provided in the appendix (Algorithms 1 and 2 ).

sections.heading: Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate JAGG on text-to-image (T2I) benchmarks, comparing against the standard per-step GRPO baseline and an ablation variant ( Ablate ). The Ablate variant performs backward passes only on the first ( j = 0 j{=}0 ) and last ( j = W − 1 j{=}W{-}1 ) velocity predictions within each group—identical to JAGG in backward count—but assigns the full loss signal to each endpoint independently, without any Jacobian interpolation or aggregation of the intermediate steps. Concretely, it computes s 0 s_{0} and s W − 1 s_{W-1} only (discarding s 1 , … , s W − 2 s_{1},\ldots,s_{W-2} ) and issues a joint backward with equal weighting, rather than using t t -weighted aggregation. The same jagg_frac schedule is applied, making this a controlled ablation that isolates the contribution of the two-endpoint Jacobian interpolation. All experiments use a window size of W = 4 W=4 and jagg_frac = 0.6 =0.6 unless noted. We report HPSv2.1 ( Wu et al. 2023 ) , PickScore ( Kirstain et al. 2023 ) , and CLIPScore ( Hessel et al. 2022 ) as evaluation metrics, along with wall-clock step time to quantify training efficiency. Setup. T2I models (QwenImage, Flux) are trained on 8 GPUs each with 270 GB of memory and connected via high-speed interconnect. All inference is performed on the same 8 GPUs . T2I quality metrics are computed on the official HPSv2.1 test set ( Wu et al. 2023 ) .

sections.heading: Efficiency Analysis on DanceGRPO
sections.text: Under DanceGRPO, JAGG reduces the mean per-step wall-clock time from 279 s → \rightarrow 228 s on Flux ( 18.2% speedup) and from 835 s → \rightarrow 691 s on QwenImage ( 17.3% speedup). The core efficiency gain of JAGG is the reduction of transformer backward passes from W W per group to 2 2 ; for W = 4 W=4 this yields a ∼ \sim 2 × \times backward-pass reduction. Two factors further amplify each backward pass beyond its raw FLOPs—(i) the backward of a transformer layer costs roughly 2 × 2\times its forward, and (ii) every backward triggers an all-reduce/reduce-scatter over the full parameter gradient tensor under DP/FSDP. A detailed derivation of these two effects (attention-backward FLOP accounting via Eqs. ( 16 )–( 19 ) and the communication analysis) is provided in Appendix B .

sections.heading: Text-to-Image Generation based on Flow-GRPO-Fast
sections.text: To validate the robustness of our method accross different RL Algorithms for DiT models, we also apply JAGG to the Flow-GRPO-Fast algorithm ( Liu et al. 2025a ) . We trained different recipe on QwenImage ( Wu et al. 2025 ) and Flux1.dev ( Liu et al. 2025a ) models with HPSv2.1 and CLIPScore rewards (1:1 ratio). In this experiment, we run our ablation method on Flux1.dev. The training recipe is almost the same as the ones in DanceGRPO. Figure 9 is the reward curve of the training of two models. Figure 3 reports the evaluation results measured every 10 training steps for Flux1.dev, and Figure 4 shows the corresponding results for QwenImage. Figure 3: Flux1.dev validate reward curve trained using Flow-GRPO-Fast algorithm under different settings (w JAGG, w/o JAGG, Ablation). Figure 4: QwenImage validate reward curve trained using Flow-GRPO-Fast algorithm under different settings (w JAGG, w/o JAGG, Ablation). Overall, the Flow-GRPO-Fast experiments show that JAGG preserves the reward optimization behavior of the original algorithm while improving the effectiveness of the policy update. For Flux1.dev, JAGG closely follows the non-accelerated baseline on HPSv2.1 and achieves a clear advantage on CLIPScore in the middle and later stages of training, which leads to the best average reward over most checkpoints. The ablation variant is consistently weaker than full JAGG, especially on the averaged metric, indicating that simply back-propagating through two endpoints is insufficient; the intermediate-step gradient information recovered by Jacobian aggregation is important for stable reward improvement. PickScore exhibits larger fluctuations because it is evaluated in an out-of-distribution setting, but JAGG remains comparable to the baseline and does not introduce systematic degradation. For QwenImage, the benefit of JAGG is even more pronounced in the later training stage. Although the baseline initially improves faster, its HPSv2.1, PickScore, and CLIPScore curves start to decline after the middle checkpoints, suggesting a less stable optimization trajectory. In contrast, JAGG continues to improve or remain stable after step 80 and eventually obtains substantially higher HPSv2.1, PickScore, and average reward. This trend suggests that JAGG is not merely a computational shortcut: by aggregating the gradient signals across the denoising window, it can produce a smoother and more reliable update direction under Flow-GRPO-Fast as well. Together with the Flux1.dev results, these curves demonstrate that JAGG generalizes beyond DanceGRPO and remains effective across different DiT backbones and RL training recipes.

sections.heading: Efficiency Analysis on Flow-GRPO-Fast
sections.text: We measure the wall-clock cost of one training iteration under the Flow-GRPO-Fast recipe on both QwenImage and Flux1.dev. Figure 5 reports both the end-to-end mean per-step time (left) and the per-step update time (right). Here “update” refers to the full policy-update stage that JAGG targets: it consists of (i) a forward pass on the stored experience (rolled-out latents and old log-probabilities) to reconstruct the current-policy log-probabilities and the surrogate loss, and (ii) the backward pass that produces the parameter gradients. JAGG only alters this update stage—the rollout, reward evaluation, optimizer step, and communication schedule are unchanged. JAGG reduces the mean step time from 674 s → \rightarrow 556 s on QwenImage (17.5% speedup) and 316 s → \rightarrow 272 s on Flux1.dev (13.9% speedup). The update time alone drops from 393 s → \rightarrow 275 s on QwenImage (30.0% speedup) and 144 s → \rightarrow 101 s on Flux1.dev (29.9% speedup). The much larger reduction on the update stage relative to the full step confirms that the savings come from replacing the per-timestep forward+backward passes with JAGG’s two-endpoint schedule. Figure 5: Flow-GRPO-Fast + JAGG: Left: end-to-end mean training step time (seconds). Right: per-step update time (forward on stored experience + backward), which is the stage JAGG directly targets. Percentages above the bars indicate the wall-clock speedup of JAGG over the baseline. The end-to-end wall-clock numbers for Flow-GRPO-Fast in Figure 5 are also consistent with the DanceGRPO speedups reported above; the underlying FLOP and communication analysis is shared and detailed in Appendix B .

sections.heading: Analysis
sections.text: Why Two Endpoints Outperforms. The ablation results consistently show that JAGG outperforms the endpoint-only variant. This is expected: interpolating intermediate gradients recovers more information than discarding them. Additionally, JAGG’s linear interpolation of Jacobians effectively marginalizes out stochastic noise perturbations that cause per-step fluctuations, analogous to replacing an SDE trajectory with its deterministic ODE skeleton ( Li et al. 2026 ) , which may explain why JAGG occasionally exceeds the exact baseline. Effect of jagg_frac . The jagg_frac hyperparameter controls what fraction of denoising groups use JAGG versus exact per-step backward. We set it via the cos ≥ 0.5 \cos\geq 0.5 threshold from the gradient quality analysis (“ Appendix E Empirical Gradient Quality and Choice of jagg_frac ” section): jagg_frac = 0.6 \texttt{jagg\_frac}=0.6 for T2I models.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: We presented JAGG, a Jacobian-aggregation framework for accelerating GRPO training of diffusion models. By exploiting the near-linearity of velocity Jacobians in the high-noise regime, JAGG reduces backward passes from W W to 2 2 per group of W W timesteps, achieving consistent wall-clock speedups (17–18% per training step) with minimal quality degradation. We provided a rigorous proof that the t t -weighted interpolation is exact under linear conditions, and demonstrated the generality of our method across multiple text-to-image diffusion backbones. JAGG represents a significant step toward making large-scale diffusion GRPO training practical, and we hope it enables more widespread adoption of RL-based alignment for visual generative models.

sections.heading: Appendix B Why Backward-Pass Reduction Yields Outsized Speedup
sections.text: This appendix expands on the two mechanisms briefly referenced in the main-text Efficiency Analysis: (i) the transformer backward pass is intrinsically more expensive than the forward pass in FLOPs, and (ii) each backward pass triggers a collective communication under data parallelism. Together they explain why cutting the number of backward passes from W W to 2 2 per group yields a wall-clock speedup that is substantially larger than what raw FLOP counts alone would suggest. Backward-pass compute is inherently heavier than forward. Consider the scaled dot-product attention sublayer. The forward pass computes: S = Q ​ K ⊤ / d k , P = softmax ​ ( S ) , O = P ​ V , S=QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d_{k}},\quad P=\text{softmax}(S),\quad O=PV, (15) where Q , K , V ∈ ℝ N × d k Q,K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{k}} . The dominant cost is the two matrix products Q ​ K ⊤ QK^{\top} and P ​ V PV , each O ⁡ ( N 2 ​ d k ) O(N^{2}d_{k}) FLOPs, giving a total forward attention cost of 2 ​ N 2 ​ d k 2N^{2}d_{k} FLOPs (ignoring the cheap softmax). In the backward pass, given upstream gradient ∂ L / ∂ O \partial L/\partial O , one must compute: ∂ L ∂ V \displaystyle\frac{\partial L}{\partial V} = P ⊤ ​ ∂ L ∂ O , \displaystyle=P^{\top}\frac{\partial L}{\partial O}, (16) ∂ L ∂ P \displaystyle\frac{\partial L}{\partial P} = ∂ L ∂ O ​ V ⊤ , \displaystyle=\frac{\partial L}{\partial O}V^{\top}, (17) ∂ L ∂ S \displaystyle\frac{\partial L}{\partial S} = softmax_bwd ​ ( P , ∂ L ∂ P ) , \displaystyle=\text{softmax\_bwd}\!\left(P,\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial P}\right), (18) ∂ L ∂ Q \displaystyle\frac{\partial L}{\partial Q} = ∂ L ∂ S ​ K / d k , ∂ L ∂ K = ( ∂ L ∂ S ) ⊤ ​ Q / d k . \displaystyle=\frac{\partial L}{\partial S}K/\sqrt{d_{k}},\quad\frac{\partial L}{\partial K}=\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial S}\right)^{\top}Q/\sqrt{d_{k}}. (19) Equations ( 16 )–( 19 ) involve four O ⁡ ( N 2 ​ d k ) O(N^{2}d_{k}) matrix products (for ∂ L / ∂ V \partial L/\partial V , ∂ L / ∂ P \partial L/\partial P , ∂ L / ∂ Q \partial L/\partial Q , ∂ L / ∂ K \partial L/\partial K ) plus the O ⁡ ( N 2 ) O(N^{2}) softmax backward—totaling 4 ​ N 2 ​ d k 4N^{2}d_{k} dominant FLOPs, exactly 𝟐 × \mathbf{2\times} the forward attention cost. Accounting for the weight-gradient terms in the linear projections, the full transformer backward is approximately 2 × 2\times the forward in total FLOPs. Reducing the number of backward passes therefore yields disproportionately larger compute savings than an equal reduction in forward passes. All-reduce communication is coupled to every backward pass under data parallelism. In distributed training with data parallelism (DP) or FSDP, each backward pass triggers an all-reduce (or reduce-scatter) over the full parameter gradient tensor. This communication is unavoidable regardless of batch size: even a single-sample backward must synchronize gradients across all DP ranks before the optimizer step. In large-scale setups the all-reduce overhead is non-trivial—it grows linearly with parameter count and can constitute a significant fraction of step time at scale. Because JAGG reduces the number of backward passes from W W to 2 2 per group, it also reduces the number of all-reduce rounds by the same factor, directly cutting communication overhead. Together, these two effects account for the measured end-to-end speedups reported in the Efficiency Analysis sections (DanceGRPO and Flow-GRPO-Fast, Figure 5 ).

sections.heading: Appendix D Experimental Setup and Hyperparameters
sections.text: This section reports the full hardware and hyperparameter configuration used in our experiments. All training scripts share the same family of arguments built on top of torchrun with FSDP-wrapped DiT backbones; the only systematic differences across runs lie in (i) the underlying base model, (ii) the JAGG-specific arguments ( sum_sample , jagg_frac ), and (iii) the resolution / temporal extent imposed by the generation modality. Inference (rollout) and training share the same code path during on-policy GRPO; we therefore describe their hyperparameters jointly. Hardware. All experiments are conducted on GPUs each with 270 270 GB of memory and high-speed interconnect. Image-generation experiments (Flux, QwenImage) use a single node of 8 8 GPUs. Inference (the on-policy rollout that produces the candidate group of G = 12 G=12 samples per prompt) is uniformly carried out on 8 8 GPUs with FSDP sharding of the DiT backbone, ensuring a comparable throughput baseline across all reported wall-clock numbers. Common GRPO and optimization settings. We use AdamW with learning rate 1 × 10 − 5 1\times 10^{-5} , weight decay 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} , no warmup, and bf16 mixed precision throughout. Each step uses G = 12 G=12 generations per prompt with intra-group advantage normalization ( use_group ). The PPO-style surrogate uses a clip range of 0.1 0.1 and an advantage clamp of 5.0 5.0 , with gradient clipping at 1 × 10 − 3 1\times 10^{-3} to stabilize training under the larger effective batch size implied by gradient_accumulation_steps . All runs use seed 42, sampler seed 12627 12627 , shared initial noise ( init_same_noise / use_same_noise ) within each group, and CFG disabled ( cfg=0.0 ). Sampling and rollout. We use a unified denoising schedule of sampling_steps = 21 =21 across all models. The choice of 21 21 rather than 20 20 ensures that ( sampling_steps − 1 ) = 20 (\texttt{sampling\_steps}-1)=20 is divisible by the JAGG group size W ∈ { 4 , 5 } W\in\{4,5\} , which is required for clean grouping. The flow-matching shift parameter is 3 3 for image models, with stochastic-DDIM noise scale η = 0.3 \eta=0.3 (Flux JAGG additionally uses η = 0.9 \eta=0.9 for higher exploration). The image runs render at 720 × 720 720\times 720 ( t = 1 t=1 ). Per-experiment configuration. Table 4 reports the per-model settings for QwenImage and Flux. Within each model the standard baseline and the JAGG variant share the same hyperparameters; the only differences are the JAGG-specific arguments ( sum_sample , jagg_frac , JAGG variant), which are inactive in the baseline and listed at the bottom of the table. Per-GPU batch size is 8 8 throughout; the effective on-policy batch size per optimizer step is train_batch_size × \times nproc × \times gradient_accumulation_steps divided by sp_size . To verify that this transfers to real diffusion backbones—and in particular to confirm that JAGG provides accurate gradient estimates in the early, high-noise denoising steps —we directly measure the approximation quality on rollouts from Flux and QwenImage. For each rollout we use 20 20 denoising steps split into 5 5 groups of W = 4 W{=}4 . As shown in Table 5 , in the high-noise groups (0–1) JAGG produces gradients very close to the exact reference on both backbones—cosine similarities are 0.85 0.85 / 0.77 0.77 (Flux) and 0.79 0.79 / 0.64 0.64 (QwenImage), with norm ratio ρ \rho within ± 50 % \pm 50\% of 1 1 . This confirms the central premise of JAGG: in the early denoising steps the velocity field is sufficiently close to linear that two-endpoint Jacobian aggregation recovers the true descent direction faithfully. The approximation degrades monotonically as noise decreases, with cosine similarity dropping below 0.7 0.7 at group 3 for both T2I models, while ρ \rho inflates dramatically in later groups—reaching 4.35 × 4.35\times at group 4 for QwenImage—precisely the signal that motivates the joint routing rule to exclude these groups. This measurement directly determines jagg_frac : we route a group to JAGG when its measured cos ⁡ ( g ^ JAGG , g exact ) ≥ 0.5 \cos(\hat{g}_{\text{JAGG}},g_{\text{exact}})\geq 0.5 . A cosine similarity above 0.5 0.5 ensures that the approximated gradient has a positive projection onto the true descent direction, and optimization theory ( Bottou, Curtis, and Nocedal 2018 ) establishes that such a sufficient-descent-direction condition is sufficient for convergence of gradient-based methods; our training uses Adam/AdamW which, as a preconditioned SGD-with-momentum optimizer, inherits the same robustness to biased gradient directions. Applying this rule: for Flux, groups 0–3 all exceed 0.5 0.5 in mean cosine, though group 3 carries high variance ( ± 0.13 \pm 0.13 ); we conservatively set jagg_frac = 0.6 =0.6 (groups 0–2) to avoid the borderline group 3. For QwenImage, groups 0–2 qualify, also yielding jagg_frac = 0.6 =0.6 . This data-driven rule exactly reproduces the values used in our main experiments and provides a model-agnostic recipe for any new backbone.

While successful in large language models ( Shao et al. 2024 ) , its extension to diffusion and flow matching models introduces a severe computational bottleneck: gradients must be back-propagated through the high-capacity DiT backbone at every timestep of the sampling trajectory, making high-resolution text-to-image (T2I) training prohibitively expensive. Training-free DiT inference acceleration methods (e.g., Δ \Delta -DiT, ScalingCache) exploit the fact that DiT hidden states and velocity predictions vary smoothly and nearly linearly along the trajectory. We ask whether the same linearity can reduce the backward-pass cost of DiT RL training, and answer affirmatively with JAGG ( J acobian- A ggregated G roup G radient), which reduces full transformer backward passes from W W to 2 2 per group of W W consecutive steps. Initially proposed in the context of large language models (LLMs) ( Shao et al. 2024 ) , GRPO eliminates the need for a separate value network by normalizing advantages within a group of candidate responses sampled from the same policy. This design significantly reduces the memory and computational overhead compared to Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), making online RL training practical for large-scale autoregressive models. The success of GRPO in mathematical reasoning ( Shao et al. 2024 ) , long-context tasks ( Ping et al. 2026 ) , and multimodal alignment ( Wang et al. 2026b ) has spurred interest in extending the paradigm beyond language. More recently, GRPO has been adapted to diffusion-based visual generation, where it has shown promising results in improving image quality, text alignment, and aesthetic preference. Two pioneering works—DanceGRPO ( Xue et al. 2025 ) and Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al. 2025a ) —demonstrated that applying GRPO to diffusion transformers (DiTs) and flow matching models can substantially enhance generation quality. Both methods treat the denoising process as a multi-step decision-making problem, computing a policy gradient loss at each timestep of the sampling trajectory. However, this per-step formulation introduces a severe computational bottleneck: standard training requires one full forward + backward pass through the denoising network for every timestep in each training window. For high-resolution text-to-image (T2I) generation, where sampling trajectories typically span dozens of steps, this leads to prohibitively expensive training. The key distinguishing feature of DiT RL, compared to language model RL, is that the “actions” are entire high-dimensional denoising steps, and the policy must be optimized over long multi-step trajectories that unfold through the DiT backbone. This structure imposes an unavoidable requirement: gradients must be back-propagated through the denoising network at every timestep of the trajectory in order to update model parameters. Unlike language models, where each token step is lightweight, each backward pass through a modern DiT incurs the full cost of a transformer forward pass, making the per-step backward requirement the dominant training expense . Interestingly, this same trajectory structure has been extensively studied in the context of training-free DiT inference acceleration. A line of work has observed that the hidden states, attention outputs, and velocity predictions of DiTs vary smoothly and nearly linearly along the denoising trajectory : consecutive denoising steps produce similar intermediate representations that can be reused, cached, or extrapolated with minimal quality loss. Methods such as Δ \Delta -DiT ( Chen et al. 2024b ) , Pyramid Attention Broadcast ( Zhao et al. 2025b ) , TaylorSeers ( Liu et al. 2025b ) , and ScalingCache ( Gu et al. 2026 ) all exploit this trajectory smoothness to skip or approximate network evaluations at intermediate timesteps, achieving substantial inference speedups with negligible quality degradation. This raises a natural question: can the same trajectory linearity that benefits training-free inference acceleration also be exploited to reduce the backward-pass cost in DiT RL training? If the Jacobians of the denoising velocity field with respect to model parameters vary linearly along the trajectory—mirroring the observed smoothness of the forward activations—then the expensive per-step backward passes could be replaced by cheap interpolations, reducing the total number of full network backward passes from W W to a small constant. In this work, we address the efficiency challenge of diffusion GRPO training. We propose JAGG ( J acobian- A ggregated G roup G radient), a mathematically principled acceleration method that reduces the number of network backward passes from W W to 2 2 for a group of W W consecutive denoising steps. Our key insight is that the Jacobian of the denoising velocity field v θ ​ ( z , t ) v_{\theta}(z,t) with respect to model parameters θ \theta is approximately linear in the inputs ( z , t ) (z,t) during the high-noise regime, which permits accurate interpolation of intermediate-step Jacobians from only the endpoint Jacobians. We provide a formal proof that this interpolation is exact when the velocity is strictly linear, and demonstrate empirically that the approximation holds with negligible error under practical training conditions. We validate JAGG on T2I benchmarks, demonstrating consistent acceleration with negligible degradation in generation quality. Our contributions are: • We identify and formalize the computational bottleneck in diffusion GRPO training, arising from per-timestep backward passes across the sampling trajectory. • We propose JAGG, a Jacobian-aggregation framework that reduces backward passes from W W to 2 2 per group, grounded in a rigorous theoretical analysis of the linearity of velocity Jacobians. • We prove that under linear velocity conditions, the t t -weighted Jacobian interpolation is exact with zero approximation error. • We demonstrate the generality of our method through extensive experiments on text-to-image generation tasks across multiple diffusion backbones. Related Work Diffusion, Flow Matching, and RL Fine-tuning. Diffusion models ( Ho, Jain, and Abbeel 2020 ; Song, Meng, and Ermon 2022 ) and rectified-flow matching ( Liu, Gong, and Liu 2022 ) underpin modern visual generation, with surveys of their interplay with RL in ( Zhu et al. 2024 ; Du et al. 2024 ) . Early RL-based fine-tuning frames denoising as a multi-step decision process (DDPO ( Black et al. 2024 ) ), and follow-ups explore preference optimization (DPOK ( Fan et al. 2023 ) , DiffPO ( Chen et al. 2025 ) ), KL-regularized PPO (DiffPPO ( Xiao et al. 2024 ) ), text-encoder RL (TexForce ( Chen et al. 2024a ) ), and diversity-oriented RL ( Miao et al. 2024 ) . GRPO for Visual Generation. DanceGRPO ( Xue et al. 2025 ) and Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al. 2025a ) first adapted GRPO to diffusion/flow models, with follow-ups on unified reasoning-driven optimization (UniGRPO ( Liu et al. 2026 ) ), stability via branching (BranchGRPO ( Li et al. 2025 ) ) or clip regulation (GRPO-Guard ( Wang et al. 2025 ) ), ODE/SDE mixing (MixGRPO ( Li et al. 2026 ) ), credit assignment (PCPO ( Lee and Ye 2026 ) ), and extensions to masked ( Luo et al. 2026 ) , autoregressive ( Yuan et al. 2025 ) , and discrete ( Wang et al. 2026a ; Ma et al. 2025 ) generators, video RL ( Zheng et al. 2026b ) , simplified online RL for denoisers (V-GRPO ( Tang et al. 2026 ) ), forward-process alignment (DiffusionNFT ( Zheng et al. 2026a ) ), likelihood-estimation design ( Choi et al. 2026 ) , and black-box distillation (PRISM ( Wang et al. 2026b ) ). Beyond images, GRPO has also been applied to diffusion language models ( Zhong et al. 2026 ; Rojas et al. 2026 ; Zhao et al. 2025a ) . Existing accelerations of the GRPO backward pass—stochastic backward in DanceGRPO ( Xue et al. 2025 ) , restricted SDE windows in Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al. 2025a ) and MixGRPO ( Li et al. 2026 ) , and merged trajectories in BranchGRPO ( Li et al. 2025 ) —are heuristic and discard much per-step gradient information; we instead faithfully approximate the full backward-pass signal at a substantially lower cost. GRPO in Language Models. GRPO originated in DeepSeekMath ( Shao et al. 2024 ) and was later extended to long-context reasoning ( Ping et al. 2026 ) and connected to classification-style RLVR ( Zhai et al. 2026 ) ; see ( Zhang et al. 2025 ) for a broader survey. Unlike inference-time acceleration (distillation, consistency models), our work is orthogonal and targets the backward-pass bottleneck specific to diffusion GRPO. The sequential variant keeps at most one computation graph in memory at any time, at the cost of two separate FSDP all-gathers (one per backward). In practice we use the joint variant for T2I models, reserving the sequential variant for cases where peak memory is critical. Both variants produce identical gradients and achieve the same ∼ \sim 2 × \times backward speedup. The full pseudocode for both variants is provided in the appendix (Algorithms 1 and 2 ). Experiments We evaluate JAGG on text-to-image (T2I) benchmarks, comparing against the standard per-step GRPO baseline and an ablation variant ( Ablate ). The Ablate variant performs backward passes only on the first ( j = 0 j{=}0 ) and last ( j = W − 1 j{=}W{-}1 ) velocity predictions within each group—identical to JAGG in backward count—but assigns the full loss signal to each endpoint independently, without any Jacobian interpolation or aggregation of the intermediate steps. Concretely, it computes s 0 s_{0} and s W − 1 s_{W-1} only (discarding s 1 , … , s W − 2 s_{1},\ldots,s_{W-2} ) and issues a joint backward with equal weighting, rather than using t t -weighted aggregation. The same jagg_frac schedule is applied, making this a controlled ablation that isolates the contribution of the two-endpoint Jacobian interpolation. All experiments use a window size of W = 4 W=4 and jagg_frac = 0.6 =0.6 unless noted. We report HPSv2.1 ( Wu et al. 2023 ) , PickScore ( Kirstain et al. 2023 ) , and CLIPScore ( Hessel et al. 2022 ) as evaluation metrics, along with wall-clock step time to quantify training efficiency. Setup. T2I models (QwenImage, Flux) are trained on 8 GPUs each with 270 GB of memory and connected via high-speed interconnect. All inference is performed on the same 8 GPUs . T2I quality metrics are computed on the official HPSv2.1 test set ( Wu et al. 2023 ) . The core efficiency gain of JAGG is the reduction of transformer backward passes from W W per group to 2 2 ; for W = 4 W=4 this yields a ∼ \sim 2 × \times backward-pass reduction. Two factors further amplify each backward pass beyond its raw FLOPs—(i) the backward of a transformer layer costs roughly 2 × 2\times its forward, and (ii) every backward triggers an all-reduce/reduce-scatter over the full parameter gradient tensor under DP/FSDP. Overall, the Flow-GRPO-Fast experiments show that JAGG preserves the reward optimization behavior of the original algorithm while improving the effectiveness of the policy update. For Flux1.dev, JAGG closely follows the non-accelerated baseline on HPSv2.1 and achieves a clear advantage on CLIPScore in the middle and later stages of training, which leads to the best average reward over most checkpoints. The ablation variant is consistently weaker than full JAGG, especially on the averaged metric, indicating that simply back-propagating through two endpoints is insufficient; the intermediate-step gradient information recovered by Jacobian aggregation is important for stable reward improvement. PickScore exhibits larger fluctuations because it is evaluated in an out-of-distribution setting, but JAGG remains comparable to the baseline and does not introduce systematic degradation. For QwenImage, the benefit of JAGG is even more pronounced in the later training stage. Although the baseline initially improves faster, its HPSv2.1, PickScore, and CLIPScore curves start to decline after the middle checkpoints, suggesting a less stable optimization trajectory. In contrast, JAGG continues to improve or remain stable after step 80 and eventually obtains substantially higher HPSv2.1, PickScore, and average reward. This trend suggests that JAGG is not merely a computational shortcut: by aggregating the gradient signals across the denoising window, it can produce a smoother and more reliable update direction under Flow-GRPO-Fast as well. Together with the Flux1.dev results, these curves demonstrate that JAGG generalizes beyond DanceGRPO and remains effective across different DiT backbones and RL training recipes. Efficiency Analysis on Flow-GRPO-Fast We measure the wall-clock cost of one training iteration under the Flow-GRPO-Fast recipe on both QwenImage and Flux1.dev. Figure 5 reports both the end-to-end mean per-step time (left) and the per-step update time (right). Here “update” refers to the full policy-update stage that JAGG targets: it consists of (i) a forward pass on the stored experience (rolled-out latents and old log-probabilities) to reconstruct the current-policy log-probabilities and the surrogate loss, and (ii) the backward pass that produces the parameter gradients. JAGG only alters this update stage—the rollout, reward evaluation, optimizer step, and communication schedule are unchanged. JAGG reduces the mean step time from 674 s → \rightarrow 556 s on QwenImage (17.5% speedup) and 316 s → \rightarrow 272 s on Flux1.dev (13.9% speedup). The update time alone drops from 393 s → \rightarrow 275 s on QwenImage (30.0% speedup) and 144 s → \rightarrow 101 s on Flux1.dev (29.9% speedup). The much larger reduction on the update stage relative to the full step confirms that the savings come from replacing the per-timestep forward+backward passes with JAGG’s two-endpoint schedule. Analysis Why Two Endpoints Outperforms. The ablation results consistently show that JAGG outperforms the endpoint-only variant. This is expected: interpolating intermediate gradients recovers more information than discarding them. Additionally, JAGG’s linear interpolation of Jacobians effectively marginalizes out stochastic noise perturbations that cause per-step fluctuations, analogous to replacing an SDE trajectory with its deterministic ODE skeleton ( Li et al. 2026 ) , which may explain why JAGG occasionally exceeds the exact baseline. Effect of jagg_frac . The jagg_frac hyperparameter controls what fraction of denoising groups use JAGG versus exact per-step backward. We set it via the cos ≥ 0.5 \cos\geq 0.5 threshold from the gradient quality analysis (“ Appendix E Empirical Gradient Quality and Choice of jagg_frac ” section): jagg_frac = 0.6 \texttt{jagg\_frac}=0.6 for T2I models. Conclusion We presented JAGG, a Jacobian-aggregation framework for accelerating GRPO training of diffusion models. By exploiting the near-linearity of velocity Jacobians in the high-noise regime, JAGG reduces backward passes from W W to 2 2 per group of W W timesteps, achieving consistent wall-clock speedups (17–18% per training step) with minimal quality degradation. We provided a rigorous proof that the t t -weighted interpolation is exact under linear conditions, and demonstrated the generality of our method across multiple text-to-image diffusion backbones. JAGG represents a significant step toward making large-scale diffusion GRPO training practical, and we hope it enables more widespread adoption of RL-based alignment for visual generative models.
